newsitem.title: PORTUGAL: FOCUS-Portugal's cenbank puts country on EMU track.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS-Portugal's cenbank puts country on EMU track.

text.p: Portugal's central bank issued on Tuesday some up-beat numbers on inflation and economic growth that seemed set to strengthen the view that the country could be amongst the European elite to launch the single currency.
In its latest quarterly report, the Bank of Portugal stated baldly that the country would achieve "price stability" in 1998 and that an eight-year battle to tame inflation had been won.
It forecast that inflation, one of the yardsticks for entry to economic and monetary union (EMU), would have fallen to just two percent by next year.

"Price variations of no more than two percent...(are) considered price stability," the Bank said. "1998 will therefore constitute the year in which the process of disinflation in Portugal was concluded."

Portuguese inflation had begun the decade at around 14 percent, but by the end of 1997 it should be down to just 2.25 percent on the basis of the methodology used by the European Commission's statistics body, Eurostat, the Bank said.

Inflation, budget deficits and the level of state debt will all be taken into account when European Union leaders meet next spring to decide which countries have passed the economic tests to join the single currency at its launch in January 1999.
As far as inflation goes, the ceiling is a set at 1.5 percentage points above the average of the best-peforming three member states.
The Portuguese central bank said that a rate of 2.25 percent in 1997 would be enough to qualify.
The Bank's report covered only inflation and economic growth and did not examine state finances, the other main economic hurdle that Portugal must clear.
But its optimistic predictions about the pace of economic growth should, if confirmed, boost the government's chances of meeting its budget deficit goal, analysts said.

The central bank said that it had revised upwards its estimate for growth in 1996 to 3.3 percent, against the 2.5 percent it had initially predicted. It said output, as measured by gross domestic product (GDP), was likely to rise between 3.0 and 3.75 percent this year.
It could be more, Bank of Portugal governor Antonio de Sousa told a news conference, if the economic performance of Europe as a whole was better than currently predicted.
Faster growth takes the pressure off the budget deficit by boosting tax revenues and reeducing social welfare spending.
The government says it will cut the deficit, the gap between spending and revenues, to 2.9 percent of GDP, just inside the EMU entry limit of three percent, and down from some four percent last year.

"The forecasts of the Bank of Portugal underline the fact that things are going well and that the Bank is more and more confident that Portugal is going to pass the tests," said analyst Jose Luis Alzola of Salomon Brothers in London.
